Examples to look for: XRISM ATel #17523 (X-ray detection of 3I/ATLAS, charge-exchange), XMM-Newton observations (early Dec 2025), papers modeling the comet's plasma interaction, ion tail, tail disconnection events, or CME impacts using ENLIL, WSA-ENLIL, EUHFORIA, SWMF, HUXt, or Parker-spiral mapping; a CCMC "runs on request" or modeling effort involving Jan Deca (hybrid/PIC modeling of the comet-solar-wind interaction); Mars observations (MAVEN, Mars Express, ExoMars TGO, Tianwen-1, Perseverance) during the Oct 3 2025 Mars flyby; PSP/WISPR, SOHO/LASCO, STEREO, PUNCH, Juno or Europa Clipper, Psyche, Lucy, Hera observations; Solar Orbiter/Comet Interceptor ion-tail crossing proposals. (B) Anything published specifically about solar-wind conditions in late November to early December 2025 (solar cycle 25), e.g., the X5.1 flare of 2025-11-11 and its CME/geomagnetic storm (G4/G5 on 2025-11-12?), CMEs of 2025-11-28 to 2025-12-01, the high-speed streams in that period, in-situ values at L1 (ACE/Wind/DSCOVR) or STEREO-A, and papers/reports analyzing them (including NOAA SWPC reports, Space Weather journal papers, arXiv).

Links: [{"title":"Science with the X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM)","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.04962"},{"title":"X-Ray Images of 3I/ATLAS: XRISM and XMM-Newton Captures Interstellar Comet","url":"https://www.diyphotography.net/x-ray-images-of-3i-atlas-xrism-and-xmm-newton-captures-interstellar-comet/"},{"title":"X-Ray Images of 3I/ATLAS: XRISM and XMM-Newton Captures Interstellar Comet","url":"https://www.diyphotography.net/?p=312230"},{"title":"XRISM X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission │ JAXA","url":"https://www.xrism.jaxa.jp/en/topics/news/1208/"},{"title":"3I/ATLAS update: First X-ray detection suggests the comet behaves like its solar system counterparts","url":"https://starlust.org/3-i-atlas-update-first-x-ray-detection-suggests-the-comet-behaves-like-its-solar-system-counterparts"},{"title":"Published June 22, 2026","url":"https://zenodo.org/records/20799390"},{"title":"cometa 3i atlas emite raios x e surpreende missao xrism sima00","url":"https://en.clickpetroleoegas.com.br/cometa-3i-atlas-emite-raios-x-e-surpreende-missao-xrism-sima00/"},{"title":"Interstellar Comet 3I/Atlas Unleashes Massive X-Ray Glow Stretching 250,000 Miles Through Space","url":"https://dailygalaxy.com/2025/12/interstellar-comet-3i-atlas-unleashes-massive-x-ray-glow-stretching-250000-miles-through-space/"},{"title":"www.nacion.com","url":"https://www.nacion.com/ciencia/el-cometa-3iatlas-revela-un-hallazgo-historico-al/EFGI3JQ64JHNLASC7OUR2YGFDI/story/"}]

The search turned up consistent reports that XRISM detected X-ray emission from interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, plus one outlier.

- **Detection:** XRISM's Xtend imager observed the comet for about 17 hours between November 26 and 28, 2025, with NASA and ESA partners. It recorded a dramatic halo of X-ray emission extending about 250,000 miles—roughly the distance from Earth to the Moon. A Spanish-language report says the emission came from an area of roughly 400,000 km around the nucleus (el campo de visión cubrió una región de aproximadamente 3 millones de kilómetros cuadrados was the field of view).
- **Mechanism:** The emission is attributed to charge exchange, where solar-wind ions pick up electrons from cometary gas. One source says the spectral features are likely associated with common elements such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. The XRISM team said the observed emission may indeed arise from charge-exchange interactions between the cometary gas and the solar wind.
- **Significance:** A JAXA news item said earlier attempts to see X-rays from interstellar comets had none have been successfully detected. ESA's XMM-Newton also detected soft X-rays from the coma, and coverage describes these as the first confirmed X-ray observations of an interstellar comet.
- **Outlier:** A Zenodo preprint titled "On The X-Ray Silence of 3I/ATLAS" claims No photons were detected, no detections were reported, and no archival entries exist. It contradicts the mission and agency reports, and I found no evidence it has been peer-reviewed, so I'd treat it with skepticism.

I did not find the XRISM Astronomer's Telegram (ATel) itself, so I can't confirm its exact wording or numbers. The figures above come from secondary news coverage and the JAXA release. Check the ATel directly for the primary details.

Links: [{"title":"Ion abundances in the plasma tail of 3I/ATLAS show that it is N2-rich","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2609.05393"},{"title":"Spatial Profiles of 3I/ATLAS CN and Ni Outgassing from ...","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.11779"},{"title":"Prospects for the Crossing of Comet 3I/ATLAS's Ion Tail","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.13222"},{"title":"3I/ATLAS (C/2025 N1): Direct Spacecraft Exploration of a Possible Relic of Planetary Formation at \"Cosmic Noon\"","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.15768"},{"title":"3I/ATLAS is Leaving a Mysterious “Hidden” Trail of Particles in Its Wake—Now Scientists Have a Plan to Intercept It   - The Debrief","url":"https://thedebrief.org/3i-atlas-is-leaving-a-mysterious-hidden-trail-of-particles-in-its-wake-now-scientists-have-a-plan-to-intercept-it/"},{"title":"[2510.13222] Prospects for the Crossing of Comet 3I/ATLAS's Ion Tail","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13222"},{"title":"[2609.05393] Ion abundances in the plasma tail of 3I/ATLAS show that it is N2-rich","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05393"},{"title":"[2510.13222] Prospects for the Crossing of Comet 3I/ATLAS’s Ion Tail","url":"https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2510.13222"},{"title":"Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS's tail is still growing, new image shows","url":"https://www.space.com/stargazing/interstellar-comet-3i-atlass-tail-is-still-growing-new-image-shows"}]

The search turned up a 2026 observational paper on the ion tail and a 2025 paper on spacecraft crossings of it.

- **Ion composition (Ferellec, Opitom, Snodgrass, arXiv:2609.05393, submitted Sept. 2026):** Using WHT/WEAVE-LIFU data from late November and early December 2025, the authors detected several ions in the anti-solar tail, including N2+, CO+, CO2+, H2O+, and CH+. They set a lower limit of N2/CO above 0.023, which they read as evidence that 3I/ATLAS is nitrogen-rich compared with Solar System comets. They also found only a marginal decrease in CH+ with distance from the nucleus. (We simultaneously detect the ions N2+, CO+, CO2+, H2O+ and CH+ located in an anti-solar tail.; the N2+/CO+ ratio allows us to constrain the lower-limit N2/CO>0.023+/-0.001)

- **Spacecraft crossing predictions (Grant & Jones, arXiv:2510.13222, Oct. 2025):** The authors used their Tailcatcher model to predict that Europa Clipper and Hera could be immersed in the ion tail in late October to early November 2025. They also expected solar wind changes, possibly a magnetic draping structure around the comet. (Hera will possibly be immersed within the ion tail of 3I/ATLAS during the period 25 October - 1 November 2025.; a magnetic draping structure associated with the comet may be identifiable.)

- **Solar wind context:** One source notes that the solar wind is much faster (typically 400 km s-1 or faster), and supersonic, so that ion tails are typically radially aligned in the anti-Sun direction.

- **Tail development (Keck KCWI, arXiv:2510.11779):** This paper reports that the comet indeed developed an anti-solar tail as of late August. It focuses on CN and Ni outgassing rather than the solar wind itself.

I did not check whether the Grant & Jones spacecraft predictions were confirmed by actual observations; the results I found don't say.

**Authors:** Samuel R. Grant, Geraint H. Jones

**Title:** Prospects for the Crossing of Comet 3I/ATLAS's Ion Tail

**Submission date:** 15 October 2025 (v1, arXiv:2510.13222)

**Journal ref:** None listed. The comments field says the paper "will be published in RNAAS," and a related DOI (10.3847/2515-5172/ae12e6) is provided.

**Abstract (paraphrased):** The authors examine two chances for spacecraft to observe the ion tail of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS in situ. Its hyperbolic orbit lies closely aligned with the ecliptic plane, and the comet passes upstream of the Europa Clipper and Hera spacecraft in October and November 2025. The authors predict that Europa Clipper may be immersed in the ion tail from 30 October to 6 November 2025, which could reveal the signatures of an interstellar comet's ion tail. They also expect changes in the solar wind and possibly a magnetic draping structure around the comet that could be identifiable. Hera may be immersed in the tail from 25 October to 1 November 2025.

**Solar wind values:** None. The paper mentions expected solar wind changes but gives no numerical values for speed, density, IMF, or other parameters.

The search didn't turn up a published result confirming that Europa Clipper actually passed through 3I/ATLAS's ion tail. What it did turn up:

- **The prediction:** Grant and Jones modeled a window of October 30 to November 6, 2025, when Europa Clipper will potentially be immersed within the ion tail of 3I/ATLAS. Their work also expected characteristic changes to the solar wind, possibly including a magnetic draping structure.
- **The caveat:** One outlet noted that the model is only as accurate as the solar wind data, which typically is only collected definitively ex post facto. The predicted miss distance was still roughly 8 million for Europa Clipper km from the tail's central axis.
- **Clipper's actual observation:** Clipper's Europa Ultraviolet Spectrograph imaged the comet on November 6, 2025, from a distance of 164 million kilometers. It detected the spectral fingerprints of oxygen, hydrogen and dust. This was a remote UV observation, not an in-situ plasma measurement.
- **Juice as a parallel dataset:** Juice collected its observations between November 5 and November 25, 2025, and scientists began analyzing the observations only in the second half of February 2026. Juice imaging mapped both a traditional dust tail and a distinct ion tail, and researchers also observed plasma interactions that visibly altered the ion tail's structure. The SETI source says these results remain preliminary.
- **Gap:** A SETI article on Clipper's UV data said whether Clipper's plasma instruments and magnetometers detected ion-tail signatures was still an open question. I didn't find a published answer to that in these results.

For a definitive answer on the in-situ crossing, I'd check NASA/JPL Europa Clipper updates or a 2026 paper from the Clipper plasma or magnetometer teams.

Prospects for the Crossing of Comet 3I/ATLAS’s Ion Tail
Samuel R. Grant
1 and Geraint H. Jones
2
1Finnish Meteorological Institute
Erik Palm´enin aukio 1, 00560 Helsinki, Finland
2European Space Agency, European Space Research and Technology Centre
Keplerlaan 1, 2201 AZ Noordwijk, The Netherlands
ABSTRACT
During October - November 2025, interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, will pass upstream
of the Europa Clipper and Hera spacecraft. Here, we identify two potential oppor-
tunities for in-situ observations of 3I’s ion tail by immersion, facilitated by the close
alignment between the comet’s hyperbolic trajectory with the ecliptic plane. During
the period 30 October - 6 November 2025, it is predicted that Europa Clipper will po-
tentially be immersed within the ion tail of 3I/ATLAS, providing the opportunity to
detect the signatures of an interstellar comet’s ion tail. Characteristic changes to the
solar wind are also expected to be observed; a magnetic draping structure associated
with the comet may be identifiable. It is further predicted that spacecraft Hera will
possibly be immersed within the ion tail of 3I/ATLAS during the period 25 October
- 1 November 2025.
Keywords: Interstellar objects (52) — Long period comets (933) — Solar wind (1534)
— Space probes (1545) — Comet ion tails (2313)
Interstellar objects are rare visitors to the Solar System, with only three observed
within the last decade. The first, 1I/’Oumuamua, had no visible coma or outgassing
throughout its passage (’Oumuamua Team et al. 2019). In contrast, 2I/Borisov had
formed a distinct blue coma and ion tail as it reached its perihelion on 8 December
2019 (Xing et al. 2020).
Comet 3I/ATLAS (C/2025 N1 (ATLAS)) is the third known interstellar object to
transit the Solar System (Seligman et al. 2025). Discovered on 1 July 2025, 3I/ATLAS
will reach a perihelion distance of 1.36 au around noon UTC on 29 October 2025.
Following a retrograde hyperbolic trajectory near the ecliptic, 3I/ATLAS has been

samuel.grant@fmi.fi
arXiv:2510.13222v1  [astro-ph.EP]  15 Oct 2025
2
observed to have an extensive coma increasing in luminosity (Meech & Fenske 2025;
Eubanks et al. 2025). Initial polarimetric observations show the comet is unique and
distinct from local comets (Gray et al. 2025).
Opportunities for observations during 3I/ATLAS’s transit of the Solar System are
collated by Eubanks et al. (2025). Conditions for observations from near Earth are
poor, but as noted by Eubanks et al. (2025), several spacecraft elsewhere could ob-
serve it. Here, we build on Eubank and co-authors’ work by providing quantitative
information on the possibility of spacecraft crossing for the first time the tail of an
interstellar comet.
Serendipitous ion tail crossings are uncommon events, although several have been
catalogued, e.g. Jones et al. (2000); Gloeckler et al. (2004); Matteini et al. (2021);
Jones et al. (2022), including likely crossings by Earth (Russell et al. 1988; Grant &
Jones 2024). Such encounters occur when a comet crosses the Sun-spacecraft line on
a timeframe such that the solar wind (SW) may transport ions at several hundred km
s−1 from the comet’s coma to a spacecraft. It is likely that many ion tail crossings have
passed unnoticed, as identification based solely on in-situ data is difficult. Without
context, ion tails’ signatures can appear as minor fluctuations in the ambient SW and
Heliospheric Magnetic Field. When ions from a comet are detected directly, then the
identification is clearer, e.g. Neugebauer et al. (2007).
The Tailcatcher program predicts and locates cometary and planetary ion tail en-
counters. The degree of alignment is quantified by the calculation of the “impact
parameter”. For past crossings, SW velocities downstream of a comet are used to
interpolate the SW flow from the spacecraft back towards the Sun. For predictions,
typical SW velocities are assumed. The impact parameter is defined by the mini-
mum miss distance from the calculated flow stream to the comet position, and is
minimised at closest alignment. Tailcatcher was successfully tested with all known
ion tail crossings, and successfully predicted three ion tail encounters (Jones et al.
2020; Grant et al. 2022; Grant & Jones 2024). Fig. 1 displays miss distances from
comet 3I/ATLAS calculated via Tailcatcher for 3 radial SW speeds for Europa Clip-
per (Korth et al. 2025). Assuming a perfectly radial flow, higher SW speeds result in
earlier and smaller predicted minimum distances from the ion tail axis. In reality, the
SW often has significant non-radial components. This can lead to closer or further
minimum impact parameters relative to the tail core; this can be assessed after the
crossing with measured SW flow vectors. Note that calculations presented here are
for the ion tail’s main axis; as the tails of active comets can be wide, an encounter
with a tail flank of is possible even if its axis is not crossed. The neutral hydrogen
corona that surrounds a comet can measure several million km across, and in some
cases, tens of millions of km (Jones et al. 2022). The minimum miss distance for SW
’packets’ is ∼(8.0)×106 km for the dates 30 October – 6 November 2025, assuming
purely radial flow. From 18 - 20 August 2025, when 3I/ATLAS was at a heliocen-
tric distance of 2.9 au, the water production rate estimated by Xing et al. (2025) was

(1.36±0.35)×1027s−1, quite high for a comet then beyond 2.5 au. Should 3I continue
to increase in activity as it approaches perihelion, a broad ion tail is possible, making
detection more likely. Spacecraft Hera (Michel et al. 2025) is similarly well-aligned
with 3I/ATLAS, with its impact parameter reaching a minimum of ∼(8.2)×106 km
during 25 October – 1 November 2025. We note that these calculations are for the
comet’s ion tail only. No operating spacecraft are expected to be in locations where
they could detect dust from 3I.
The encounters described here may be the first direct immersion in material from
an interstellar object. Even if pick-up ion measurement is not possible, magnetic
field draping and shock signatures can reveal the presence and structure of an ion
tail. Europa Clipper carries instruments for plasma (Westlake et al. 2023) and a
magnetometer (Kivelson et al. 2023), but Hera is not equipped to detect ions nor the
HMF (Eubanks et al. 2025). With favourable SW conditions, Europa Clipper has a
rare opportunity to sample an interstellar object’s tail.
It is likely that knowledge of such encounters will become more common as the
discovery rate of these objects improves.
If a similar object is discovered with a
favourable trajectory, the object itself could be encountered at closer range by ESA’s
Comet Interceptor spacecraft (Jones et al. 2024).

**Abstract (paraphrased)**
The authors note that interstellar objects let us compare planet formation in the Solar System with that around other stars. They used WHT/WEAVE-LIFU integral-field observations of 3I/ATLAS taken post-perihelion on 30 November and 2 December 2025. They detected five ions in the anti-solar tail: N2+, CO+, CO2+, H2O+, and CH+. Using common fluorescence factors, they derived abundance ratios. The N2+/CO+ ratio gives a lower limit of N2/CO > 0.023 ± 0.001, which they read as "indicating that 3I/ATLAS is N2-rich" compared with Solar System comets. They link this to cold formation conditions. The other ion ratios don't directly constrain neutral abundances but appear consistent with the object being enriched in hypervolatiles. Finally, the ratios show at most a marginal decrease in CH+ with cometocentric distance along the tail.

I found no results that model 3I/ATLAS's solar wind environment with ENLIL, EUHFORIA, HUXt, or SWMF, so the search doesn't answer your question directly. It did turn up background on the models and on the comet's perihelion.

**The comet's perihelion:** Sources disagree slightly on the date. One says Comet 3I/ATLAS is hitting a major milestone on Oct. 30, 2025. Wikipedia lists Last perihelion: 29 October 2025 11:45 UT. The closest approach was roughly within 1.4 astronomical units (AU) of the Sun. That means perihelion was almost a year ago, and any solar wind modeling would be historical.

**The models:**
- **EUHFORIA** is a physics-based solar wind and CME propagation model designed for space weather studies and forecasting purposes. Its coronal part uses the WSA model, which employs the synoptic maps of the line-of-sight photospheric magnetic field to compute the plasma parameters at 0.1 au.
- **ENLIL** is described as a comparable model. One source notes that in contrast to ENLIL which gives the background solar wind parameters for a full Carrington rotation, EUHFORIA provides daily runs.
- **HUXt** is a faster, simpler approach. It neglects magnetic and plasma pressure and treats the solar wind as a 1‐dimensional inviscid and incompressible flow. One source reports that HUXt requires approximately 0.05 seconds on a modest desktop CPU, compared with much longer runs for full MHD models.
- **SWMF** is not described in any of the results beyond a passing mention alongside the other MHD models.

If you want the comet-specific modeling, try a search that names the paper or the research group directly, or search for "interstellar comet solar wind simulation."
